# Research: Capability-narrowing grants — macaroons, Biscuit and CaMeL

**Status:** Complete  
**Date:** 2026-11-09  
**Scope:** Phase 4, Step 4.3, web-03 only  
**Delivery:** Complete report returned inline under the user-approved adaptation. No report, task, source, configuration or runtime state was changed.

**Parent persistence destination:** `/home/coder/workspaces/worktrees/IronClaude/fix-flaky-parallel-thread-test/.dev/tasks/to-do/TASK-RESEARCH-sub-orchestrator-mode-20261108-181115/research/web-03-capability-narrowing-tokens.md`

## Summary

**Macaroons and Biscuit make the narrowing-token part of issue #339 technically credible. Neither makes the proposed orchestration system “trustless,” makes an arbitrary shell hook a non-bypassable enforcement boundary, or establishes the authority to delegate operations that current policy forbids.** Biscuit is the stronger candidate for further comparison where independent receivers should verify credentials without holding the issuer’s signing secret. This is a research preference, not an adoption or implementation decision. Sources: [macaroons publication](https://research.google/pubs/macaroons-cookies-with-contextual-caveats-for-decentralized-authorization-in-the-cloud/), [Biscuit specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for mechanism documentation; recommendation is an inference.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**CaMeL addresses a different problem:** separating trusted planning from untrusted content and enforcing information-flow policies before tool execution. It is relevant to why a signed, legitimately issued grant does not prevent a compromised agent from misusing permitted authority. It is not a competing signed delegation-token format. Sources: [CaMeL paper, §§3–7](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.18813v2), [authors’ implementation](https://github.com/google-research/camel-prompt-injection). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, primary paper and authors’ repository.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The repository’s existing WC-9 precedent supplies **explicit human authorization, narrow Task scope, operational conditions and termination at that Task’s completion**. It does not supply cryptographic verification, transferable child authority, general replay prevention or revocation infrastructure. That distinction follows from the directly read contract source, indexed below as **L1**.

## Method, provenance and evidence boundaries

- Read the exact Step 4.3 prompt and ensuring clauses before other investigation.
- Read research01, research04—including its B1/B2 correction addendum—research08 and the current gaps register.
- Read issue #339 and its comments through the requested fork-explicit, read-only GitHub command.
- Checked local assertions against contract, hook, dependency-manifest and installed Orca source.
- Tavily search/extract tools, including namespace aliases, were **not present in this session’s callable tool inventory**. This meets the `tavily-unavailable` fallback condition. Every external finding below identifies its source and carries the required fallback provenance comment.
- External queries contained generic mechanism or library terms only. No private issue text, repository text, paths or source excerpts were submitted to external search/fetch tools.
- No agents, messaging, GitHub mutations, model changes, installations, tests, live orchestration experiments or implementation work were performed.

**Important extraction limitation:** the author-hosted original macaroon PDF was fetched, but WebFetch returned unreadable PDF content; local PDF rendering/text tools were unavailable. Macaroon findings therefore distinguish the directly readable original publication abstract, indexed passages from the original paper, and readable implementation documentation. This is not represented as a full-paper read. Source: [original paper PDF](https://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf). **Reliability: HIGH for the primary document; MEDIUM for the completeness of evidence extracted here.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## Issue #339: exact research target

**Source:** [issue #339](https://github.com/IronbellyOrg/IronClaude/issues/339), observed read-only. **Reliability: HIGH for the proposal’s wording, not evidence of implementation. Relevance: HIGH.**

The Step 3 passage reads verbatim:

> **Step 3, signed narrow grants (the trustless layer).** The Orchestrator issues each child a signed, expiring grant, in macaroon or Biscuit style, that names:
> - the one worktree and branch it covers,
> - the allowed message types and actions (for example `request_close` on this worktree only),
> - an expiry time, a session binding and a one-use nonce, so a captured message cannot be replayed.
>
> A receiver verifies the chain offline and refuses anything outside it. For the orchestrator-of-orchestrators in version 2, the top Orchestrator grants a sub-orchestrator a token for its set of worktrees; the sub-orchestrator can only narrow it further for its children. Nobody can grant more than they hold, which is the trustless property, and no human click is needed per message.

Open question 3 reads verbatim:

> 3. Macaroons or Biscuit: pick by which has a maintained Python or Node library the project already uses.

A later comment adds:

> 3) Engage in an adversarial debate about the pros/cons of each and go with teh winner

This investigation supplies evidence for that comparison. It does **not** claim to have conducted the separately requested adversarial debate.

## Finding 1 — Macaroons support decentralized narrowing, but use MACs rather than public-key signatures

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the original publication abstract; MEDIUM for indexed full-paper passages, corroborated by implementation documentation.**

The original publication describes nested, chained message authentication codes, including HMAC, and contextual caveats that restrict authorization. Indexed passages from the author-hosted paper describe holders creating more restrictive credentials without asking the target service to mint a replacement. “Signed” in the issue is therefore imprecise for the original macaroon mechanism: these are MAC-authenticated credentials, not ordinary public-key-signed tokens.

Sources: [original publication](https://research.google/pubs/macaroons-cookies-with-contextual-caveats-for-decentralized-authorization-in-the-cloud/), [original paper](https://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The readable JavaScript implementation documentation requires the original root-key bytes when verifying a macaroon. Its first-party caveat callback decides whether each condition is satisfied. Thus local verification still needs an appropriate secret and trusted interpretation of the request context; token integrity alone is insufficient.

Source: [go-macaroon JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship to this repository:** this **supports** the proposed narrowing property but **extends**, rather than implements, WC-9. It also creates an important trust distinction: distributing issuer-equivalent verification secrets is not the same arrangement as distributing public verification keys. No such macaroon verifier was established in L2–L4 or declared in L6.

## Finding 2 — Macaroon caveats require meaningful, restrictive verification

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: MEDIUM-HIGH, readable implementation documentation backed by the primary design.**

The Python documentation demonstrates exact caveat matching and general callback-based checks. It requires recognized conditions to be satisfied; a callback that accepts unknown or unsatisfied conditions defeats the intended restriction. The JavaScript implementation similarly exposes first-party checking and verification with discharge macaroons.

Sources: [pymacaroons documentation](https://github.com/ecordell/pymacaroons), [JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** worktree, branch, action and session caveats are useful only if the receiver compares them with trustworthy request facts. A value copied from the same untrusted message is not independent confirmation. This is an **inference from the verifier interface**, not a claim that the repository currently performs such checks.

Sources: [pymacaroons](https://github.com/ecordell/pymacaroons), [Biscuit authorizer-context documentation](https://python.biscuitsec.org/basic-use). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## Finding 3 — Third-party macaroon caveats exist, but offline checking does not mean every supporting operation is offline

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: MEDIUM for indexed primary-paper passages; MEDIUM-HIGH for implementation documentation.**

Indexed original-paper passages describe obtaining discharge macaroons from a designated third party and presenting them to the target service. The readable JavaScript implementation documents discharge verification, recursive discharge collection and binding discharges to the primary macaroon’s signature.

Sources: [original paper](https://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf), [JavaScript discharge APIs](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Feasibility interpretation:** a receiver can check a supplied credential and its supplied discharges locally when the necessary keys and predicate inputs are available. Obtaining a fresh third-party assertion may still require contact with that third party. “Offline verification” must not be expanded into “no dependency on fresh external evidence.”

Sources: [original paper](https://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf), [JavaScript implementation](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon). **The interpretation is an inference from these verification inputs.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** this **extends** the sketch with an explicit distinction between proof checking and proof acquisition. It does not resolve the repository’s message-interception or trusted-session-binding gaps.

## Finding 4 — Macaroon revocation is a separate policy and freshness problem

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: MEDIUM for indexed primary-paper extraction.**

The original paper’s indexed “Revocation and Versioning” section discusses short-lived credentials, state-based checks, allowlists/denylists, expiration, epoch counters and short-lived third-party discharges. It does not justify claiming immediate new revocation knowledge at a completely disconnected verifier.

Source: [original paper, Revocation and Versioning](https://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf). **The disconnected-verifier conclusion is an inference from the stated mechanisms.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** this **qualifies** Step 3. Expiry can bound a credential’s lifetime; it is not equivalent to immediately withdrawing a still-valid credential. WC-9’s Task-completion termination is a policy condition, not a demonstrated distributed revocation mechanism.

## Finding 5 — Biscuit supports public-key verification and holder-added restrictions

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official specification and language reference.**

Biscuit uses an asymmetric signature chain. A verifier checks against the expected root public key. An appendable bearer token carries the material needed to append another block, but not the issuer’s root private key. Appended checks restrict the derived credential; earlier blocks cannot simply be removed while preserving valid verification.

Sources: [Biscuit specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html), [Datalog reference](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/datalog.html). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

Default fact-provenance rules prevent ordinary later-block facts from becoming issuer-authorized grants. Every check must succeed, and authorization policies determine acceptance. Explicit trust scopes affect which origins can supply facts.

Source: [Datalog trust and authorization rules](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/datalog.html). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** this **supports** the parent-to-middle-to-child narrowing objective. Public-key verification is a meaningful advantage when receivers should not possess issuer signing authority. Correct authorizer policy remains essential; the signature chain does not choose that policy.

Neither Biscuit attenuation nor the reviewed macaroon mechanism establishes that a holder forgets or loses an earlier broader credential when deriving a narrower one. Biscuit’s specification describes producing a restricted derivative, not erasing the original. A compromised middle holder therefore remains dangerous within its original grant.

Source: [Biscuit specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html). **The retained-authority risk is an inference, not a claimed erasure feature.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## Finding 6 — Biscuit third-party blocks are not interchangeable with macaroon discharges

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official specification.**

Biscuit supports externally signed blocks. The third party receives signing context rather than necessarily receiving the whole token. External signatures are bound into the token context; authorization can explicitly trust an external signer’s key. Format and signature-payload compatibility requirements apply.

Source: [Biscuit specification, third-party blocks and scopes](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

This supplies a third-party attestation mechanism, but does not automatically impose the application’s desired requirement to obtain a particular attestation. The required check and trusted signer remain policy decisions. It is not simply the same protocol as fetching and binding macaroon discharge credentials.

Sources: [Biscuit specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html), [macaroon discharge documentation](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon). **The comparison is an inference from the two documented protocols.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** this **extends** the issue’s comparison criteria. “Supports third-party caveats” is too coarse to establish equivalent integration or library support.

## Finding 7 — Biscuit signature verification and authorization are explicitly separate

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official Python documentation.**

The Python documentation separates loading and signature verification from building an authorizer with request facts and policy, then evaluating authorization. Its expiration example supplies the current time as an authorizer fact. A timestamp inside the credential is not evidence that the receiver automatically checked a trusted clock.

Source: [Biscuit Python basic use](https://python.biscuitsec.org/basic-use). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** this directly **qualifies** Step 3’s “verifies the chain … refuses anything outside it.” The receiver needs both cryptographic verification and an authorization decision over the actual requested operation. No such Biscuit authorization path was established in the inspected repository hooks, L2–L4.

## Finding 8 — Biscuit revocation supports descendants, but distribution is external

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official revocation guide and specification.**

Biscuit exposes per-block revocation identifiers. Checking all identifiers lets revocation of an ancestor reject derived credentials containing that ancestor. Revoking a particular derived branch requires selecting the appropriate identifier, rather than treating all identifiers as interchangeable.

Sources: [revocation guide](https://www.biscuitsec.org/docs/guides/revocation/), [specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The guide leaves revocation publication, storage and distribution to the deployment. Startup snapshots and periodically refreshed lists have freshness limits. Offline verification can continue with locally available state, but a disconnected receiver cannot discover a newly published revocation.

Source: [revocation guide](https://www.biscuitsec.org/docs/guides/revocation/). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** this **supports** subtree revocation as a mechanism while leaving G42’s operational revocation question open. Offline signature checking is not a promise of immediate global revocation.

## Finding 9 — A nonce field is not sufficient for one-use or replay resistance

**Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, standards text; used as a general security precedent, not a proposed OAuth implementation.**

RFC 9449 distinguishes unique proof identifiers, bounded acceptance periods and duplicate detection. Its replay discussion explains recording accepted identifiers and rejecting repeats. It also permits nonce reuse in circumstances where duplicate tracking supplies replay protection.

Source: [RFC 9449, §§4.2–4.3 and 11.1–11.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship and inference:** placing a nonce in a signed macaroon or Biscuit is not, by itself, proof that the receiver will reject a second presentation. Strict one-use behavior requires trustworthy consumption state and race-safe rejection of repeats. Across multiple independent receivers, the scope and coordination of that state matter. Neither token-format documentation establishes the issue’s proposed one-use message channel.

Sources: [RFC 9449](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html), [Biscuit Python examples](https://python.biscuitsec.org/basic-use). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

Likewise, a session identifier inside a bearer credential is not itself proof that the presenter is that session. Authenticated presentation and trusted request binding remain separate questions.

Sources: [Biscuit bearer-token specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html), [RFC 9449, proof and replay discussion](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html). **This is a security inference, not a claim that either format provides the repository’s session binding automatically.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## Finding 10 — CaMeL controls information flow; it is not a delegation-token competitor

**Relevance: HIGH for untrusted-report handling; LOW as a direct token-format substitute. Reliability: HIGH, primary paper.**

CaMeL’s planner works from the trusted request without reading tool-returned untrusted contents. A separate data-processing model has no tool access. A restricted interpreter tracks value provenance and permitted readers, then checks policies before tool invocation. Its stricter mode also tracks additional control dependencies.

Source: [CaMeL paper, §§5.1–5.4 and 7](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.18813v2). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The reviewed paper text describes interpreter-maintained capability metadata, not a signed cross-session credential format with delegated issuance, offline chain verification, third-party discharges or revocation semantics. It therefore does not answer the macaroon-versus-Biscuit library question.

Source: [CaMeL paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.18813v2). **This is a bounded finding about the reviewed paper, not a universal claim about every capability system.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** CaMeL **supports** the need to keep untrusted reports from becoming executable instructions. It **contradicts a token-only interpretation** of that protection: authenticating a grant does not establish that an agent’s chosen permitted action was derived from trustworthy instructions.

## Finding 11 — CaMeL’s reported benchmark result is not a repository security guarantee

**Relevance: MEDIUM. Reliability: HIGH for the authors’ reported result and disclaimer.**

The June 24, 2025 v2 abstract reports 77% secure task completion versus 84% for an undefended system on AgentDojo—a seven-percentage-point task-completion difference, not a 77% attack-blocking rate. The paper’s guarantees depend on its threat model and enforced policies; its implementation is not presented as formally verified.

Sources: [v2 abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813v2), [paper, threat model and limitations](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.18813v2). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The authors’ repository explicitly states that it is not an officially supported Google product, may not be fully secure, and is not intended to receive ongoing maintenance/support.

Source: [CaMeL research repository](https://github.com/google-research/camel-prompt-injection). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Relationship:** this is research evidence for architectural separation, not an installable security assurance for current hooks or cross-session messaging.

## Finding 12 — Libraries exist, but “maintained and already used here” is not established

**Relevance: HIGH for Python; MEDIUM for the alternative Node surface. Reliability: HIGH for registry metadata and official project documentation; maintenance conclusions remain limited.**

| Candidate | Evidence actually observed | Decision implication |
|---|---|---|
| **Biscuit Python** | Registry page lists 0.4.0, released 2025-09-26. Official repository documents Rust bindings, token checking and first-/third-party blocks. [Registry](https://pypi.org/project/biscuit-python/), [repository](https://github.com/eclipse-biscuit/biscuit-python). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> | Credible Python candidate. Release metadata alone does not prove present security support or compatibility with this deployment. |
| **Biscuit Node/WASM** | Official repository documents Node/browser use, CommonJS, ECMAScript and TypeScript definitions. README’s package version is an example, not verified latest-release evidence. [Repository](https://github.com/eclipse-biscuit/biscuit-wasm), [Node documentation](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/usage/nodejs.html). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> | A real Node option exists; runtime, API and feature compatibility remain untested. |
| **Original pymacaroons** | Release page lists 0.13.0 dated 2018-02-21. README describes a mature, infrequently changing project and lists testing through older Python versions. [Registry](https://pypi.org/project/pymacaroons/0.13.0/), [repository](https://github.com/ecordell/pymacaroons). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> | Not sufficient evidence to assert current security maintenance or current-environment compatibility. Old release age alone does not prove abandonment. |
| **JavaScript macaroon implementation** | Documents verification, both macaroon formats and discharge binding. No actual recent release dates were visible in the inspected repository page. [Repository](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> | Implementation availability is established; current maintenance assurance is not. |

The official Biscuit implementation matrix marks Python third-party-block support **partial**, even though Python examples demonstrate third-party operations. This is not proof of a contradiction in executable behavior; it is a feature-completeness question that must be resolved for any selected package/version.

Sources: [implementation matrix](https://github.com/eclipse-biscuit/biscuit), [Python examples](https://python.biscuitsec.org/basic-use). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Repository relationship:** L6 does not establish existing dependency reuse for either family. Open question 3 cannot honestly be closed with “choose the library already used here.” No packages were installed or exercised.

## Required feasibility table

**All rows assess mechanisms, not an approved implementation.**

| Mechanism | Offline verification | Attenuation by a middle holder | Third-party caveats / assertions | Revocation and replay | Fit inside hook-based enforcement | What WC-9 already covers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Macaroons** | Local checking with the necessary root secret, supplied discharges and trusted predicate inputs. Fresh discharge acquisition can be online. | Holder adds restrictions without issuer reminting. This does not establish surrender of the holder’s original broader authority. | Discharge macaroons; documented binding to the primary credential. | Expiry, state or fresh assertions supply revocation policy; nonce presence alone does not supply one-use enforcement. | Credential checking is feasible in principle, but tool/command text alone does not establish trustworthy identity, resource state or complete interception. No existing verifier established in L2–L4. | Explicit human words, Task scope, conditions and termination. Not MAC authentication, transferable authority or replay/revocation infrastructure. **HIGH relevance; HIGH/MEDIUM reliability.** [Primary publication](https://research.google/pubs/macaroons-cookies-with-contextual-caveats-for-decentralized-authorization-in-the-cloud/), [paper](https://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf), [implementation](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon), L1. <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> |
| **Biscuit** | Signature chain verified with the root public key. Authorization still needs trusted context and applicable state. | Holder appends restriction blocks; default provenance rules prevent ordinary appended facts from becoming issuer grants. Earlier broader credentials are not erased. | Externally signed blocks and explicit signer trust; not identical to macaroon discharge semantics. | Per-block identifiers support ancestor/descendant revocation. Distribution is external; one-use consumption is not supplied merely by a nonce claim. | Better key-separation fit for independent verifiers, but not a drop-in authorization layer for current shell classifiers. Complete enforcement remains unverified. | Same policy precedent, but no cryptographic chain or right to pass the grant down. **HIGH relevance; HIGH reliability.** [Specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html), [revocation](https://www.biscuitsec.org/docs/guides/revocation/), [Python authorization](https://python.biscuitsec.org/basic-use), L1–L4. <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> |
| **CaMeL** | Not an offline signed-token protocol. | No holder-attenuated token chain established by the reviewed paper. | No corresponding discharge/delegation-token protocol established. | No token revocation or one-use redemption protocol established. | Depends on interpreter-managed provenance, planner isolation and pre-tool policy checks; cannot be reproduced by merely recognizing a signed string in a command. | No cryptographic addition to WC-9. ## Recommendations from External Research

1. **Do not approve a sub-orchestrator mode merely because narrowing tokens exist.** Retain current WC-13/D5 authority boundaries unless deliberately changed. The external evidence establishes a credential mechanism, not trusted interception, correct destructive-action decisions, host message delivery or preserved human approval. Sources: L1–L5, L8; [Biscuit authorization model](https://python.biscuitsec.org/basic-use), [CaMeL](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.18813v2). **HIGH relevance; recommendation derived from HIGH-reliability sources.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

2. **Use Biscuit as the preferred candidate in the separately requested comparison—not as an adopted dependency.** Public-key verification and explicit provenance-aware authorization match the independent-receiver question better than spreading root MAC secrets. Keep macaroons as a serious comparator where their secret-verifier trust model is acceptable. Neither candidate has satisfied “already used here” or a complete current-maintenance assessment. Sources: L6; [Biscuit specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html), [macaroon verification API](https://github.com/go-macaroon/js-macaroon), [Python registry](https://pypi.org/project/biscuit-python/). **HIGH relevance; inference, not a completed adversarial verdict.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

3. **Carry forward four distinct decision questions:** credential authenticity/attenuation; authorization over trusted request facts; complete enforcement before effects; and lifecycle state for expiry, revocation and replay. Treating these as separate questions prevents “signed authority” from being mistaken for an authorization decision. Sources: [Biscuit specification](https://doc.biscuitsec.org/reference/specifications.html), [revocation guide](https://www.biscuitsec.org/docs/guides/revocation/), [RFC 9449](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html). **HIGH relevance; HIGH reliability.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

4. **Preserve WC-9’s narrow human-origin precedent and destructive-action safeguards.** A parent’s credential is not a person’s new Task-specific instruction, a human Ruling, or evidence that a worktree is now safe to remove. CaMeL reinforces the separate need to prevent untrusted content from steering otherwise permitted actions. Sources: L1; [CaMeL paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.18813v2), [Biscuit request-context model](https://python.biscuitsec.org/basic-use). **HIGH relevance; HIGH reliability for sources; policy recommendation is an inference.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->
